summary: This packet decomposes the Jacobian challenge: a smooth proper geometrically connected curve with a rational point, its Picard functor, the Jacobian as an abelian variety, and the Abel-Jacobi map with its universal property. None of the roadmap's named books (Hartshorne, Liu, Milne's Cornell-Silverman chapter, Mumford, BLR) is in the supplied library. The packet uses authorized public copies: six Stacks Project chapters (Picard Schemes of Curves, Algebraic Curves, Varieties, Divisors, Cohomology of Schemes, Derived Categories of Schemes; version ed88ff78), Milne's Abelian Varieties notes v2.00 (Parts I and III), and Kleiman, The Picard scheme (arXiv). It also uses the library copy of Silverman for genus one. Layer A covers O_X(D) and regular sections, Weil divisors and Cl = Pic, and degree via Euler characteristics. Layer B covers vanishing on affines, Cech cohomology and finiteness, genus and chi-form Riemann-Roch, the dualizing module with Serre duality and deg omega = 2g - 2, and H^1 vanishing in degree >= 2g - 1. Layer C covers flat base change, cohomology and base change (tag 0B91), relative effective Cartier divisors, and Hilb^d = Sym^d. Layer D covers Kleiman's comparison theorem and the Br' obstruction, rigidification, the Stacks representability argument over separably closed fields, Milne's construction with Galois descent, and Kleiman 4.8 and 5.4. Layer E covers rigidity, the tangent space and dim J = g, cube and square, [n], the dual abelian variety and polarizations, and autoduality. Layer F covers the Abel-Jacobi map, closed immersion, Abel maps from symmetric powers, the Albanese property, base change, and genus 0 and 1. All stages are partial: the duality, descent and cube imports and Mumford are unread, and the source conventions conflict with the roadmap's layer order.

nodes.title: Stacks Divisors 15.1, 15.10-15.11, 16.1: the invertible sheaf O_X(D) with its canonical section, and effective Cartier divisors as pairs (L, s) with s a regular section
nodes.statement: Let X be a scheme and D an effective Cartier divisor with invertible ideal sheaf I_D. Then O_X(D) = Hom(I_D, O_X) = I_D^{-1}, with canonical section 1_D coming from the inclusion I_D -> O_X, and O_X(-D) = I_D. D |-> O_X(D) turns addition of effective Cartier divisors into the tensor product, giving a homomorphism EffCart(X)^gp -> Pic(X), where Pic(X) is the group of isomorphism classes of invertible O_X-modules. By Lemma 15.10, 1_D is a regular section. Conversely, a regular section s of an invertible L determines a unique effective Cartier divisor D = Z(s) and a unique isomorphism O_X(D) -> L with 1_D |-> s, so D <-> (L, s) is a bijection onto isomorphism classes of pairs. Remark 15.11 gives the exact sequences 0 -> O_X -> L -> i_*(L|_D) -> 0 and 0 -> L^{-1} -> O_X -> i_*O_D -> 0. On a locally Noetherian scheme, s is regular iff it does not vanish at any associated point (16.1).

Pic(X) and invertible modules are defined in Modules, Definition 25.9 (not read); O_X(D + D') = O_X(D) (x) O_X(D') is Lemma 15.4, cited in the comments to Definition 15.1 but not read

Converse (15.10): locally s = f e with e a generator of L and f a nonzerodivisor; Z(s) is cut out by f, and 1_D |-> s determines the isomorphism.

nodes.title: Stacks Divisors 27.2-28.7: Weil divisors, Cl(X), the homomorphism Pic(X) -> Cl(X); it is injective for normal X and an isomorphism iff all local rings are UFDs
nodes.statement: Let X be a locally Noetherian integral scheme. Div(X) is the group of locally finite formal sums of prime divisors (27.2). A rational function f in R(X)^* has div(f) = sum ord_Z(f)[Z] (27.5), and Cl(X) = Div(X)/principal divisors (27.7), with presentation R(X)^* -> Div(X) -> Cl(X) -> 0. For an invertible L with nonzero meromorphic section s, div_L(s) = sum ord_{Z,L}(s)[Z] (28.4). Its class is independent of s (28.3) and additive (28.5), giving Pic(X) -> Cl(X) (28.5.1). This map is injective if X is normal (28.6). The local rings of X are UFDs iff X is normal and Pic(X) -> Cl(X) is surjective, and then Pic(X) = Cl(X) (28.7). For a smooth curve over k the local rings at closed points are DVRs, hence UFDs, so Pic(X) = Cl(X) with Weil divisors sum n_x [x] over closed points.
hypotheses: X locally Noetherian and integral
The smooth-curve application uses that O_{X,x} is a DVR at closed points of a smooth curve (argued in Stacks Picard Schemes of Curves, proof of Lemma 3.1, via Varieties 25.3 and Algebra 119.7)
Lemma 28.7 uses Divisors 16.7 (prime divisors on schemes with UFD local rings are effective Cartier) and Algebra 120.6, 120.11, 157.6; none read

proofSteps: 28.6: if div_L(s) = div(f), then t = f^{-1}s has div_L(t) = 0. Locally t is a unit in every height-one localization of a Noetherian normal domain, hence a unit (Algebra 157.6), so t trivializes L.
28.7 (1) => (2): UFD local rings are normal. A prime divisor D is an effective Cartier divisor (16.7), and O_X(D) with 1_D maps to [D].
28.7 (2) => (1): surjectivity makes every height-one prime of each local ring principal, so the local ring is a UFD (Algebra 120.6).

nodes.title: Stacks Varieties 44.1-44.14: deg L = chi(L) - chi(O_X); invariance under field extension, additivity, deg O_X(D) = dim_k Gamma(D, O_D), positivity and ampleness
nodes.statement: Let X be a proper scheme of dimension <= 1 over a field k. For an invertible L, deg(L) = chi(X, L) - chi(X, O_X), and deg(E) = chi(E) - n chi(O_X) for E locally free of rank n (44.1). Properties: (44.2) the degree is unchanged by extension of the base field; (44.3) it is additive in short exact sequences; (44.7) deg(E (x) V) = rank(E) deg(V) + rank(V) deg(E), so deg(L (x) M) = deg L + deg M and deg: Pic(X) -> Z is a homomorphism; (44.9) an effective Cartier divisor D is finite over k with deg O_X(D) = deg(D) = dim_k Gamma(D, O_D). On a proper curve (44.12): an L with a nonzero section has deg L >= 0, with equality iff L = O_X; a nonzero map N -> L forces deg L >= deg N, with equality iff it is an isomorphism. Also L is ample iff deg L > 0 (44.14). Pic^0(X) is the kernel of deg, as an abstract group.

If X is quasi-compact with affine diagonal (e.g. separated) and covered by t affine opens, then H^n(X, F) = 0 for n >= t (4.2). For f: X -> S proper over a locally Noetherian S and F coherent, R^i f_*F is coherent (19.1), and if S = Spec A with A Noetherian, H^i(X, F) is a finite A-module (19.2). For a proper curve over k: every H^i(X, F) is finite-dimensional, and H^i = 0 for i >= 2 once X is covered by two affines.

nodes.statement: Let X be proper over k of dimension 1 with H^0(X, O_X) = k. For a proper geometrically integral variety this holds by Varieties 26.2(4), and a smooth projective curve with a k-rational point has it by Picard 6.1. nodes.title: Stacks Curves 4.1-4.3, 5.1-5.2, 8.3-8.4: the dualizing module (omega_X = Omega_{X/k} for smooth X), Serre duality H^i(E)^vee = H^{1-i}(E^vee (x) omega_X), and deg omega_X = -2 chi(O_X) = 2g - 2
nodes.statement: Let X be proper of dimension <= 1 over k. There is a dualizing complex omega_X^* with the following properties: omega_X = H^{-1}(omega_X^*) is coherent Cohen-Macaulay; Ext^i(K, omega_X^*) = Hom_k(H^{-i}(X, K), k); Hom(F, omega_X) = Hom_k(H^1(X, F), k); and omega_X = Omega_{X/k} when X -> Spec k is smooth of relative dimension 1 (4.1). If X is Cohen-Macaulay and equidimensional of dimension 1, then Ext^{1+i}(F, omega_X) = Hom_k(H^{-i}(X, F), k) (4.2). Hence, for E finite locally free, Hom_k(H^{-i}(X, E), k) = H^{1+i}(X, E^vee (x) omega_X), and for L invertible h^0(L) = h^1(L^{-1} (x) omega_X) and h^1(L) = h^0(L^{-1} (x) omega_X) (Remark 4.3). If X is Gorenstein and equidimensional of dimension 1 (5.2): omega_X is invertible, deg omega_X = -2 chi(X, O_X), chi(E) = deg(E) - (1/2) rank(E) deg(omega_X), and dim H^i(E) = dim H^{1-i}(E^vee (x) omega_X). If moreover H^0(O_X) = k, then deg omega_X = 2g - 2 (8.3). For smooth X, dim H^0(Omega_{X/k}) = g and deg Omega_{X/k} = 2g - 2 (8.4).

5.2: apply chi(E) = deg(c_1(E) cap [X]_1) + rank(E) chi(O_X) to omega_X and combine with 5.1 to get 2 chi(O_X) = -deg omega_X; substitute back for general E.

nodes.statement: A relative effective Cartier divisor on X/S is an effective Cartier divisor D that is flat over S (Divisors 19.2). Its pullback along any S' -> S is again an effective Cartier divisor (19.1). Sums (19.3) and differences D_2 = D_1 + D for D_1 inside D_2 (19.4) stay relative. For X -> S flat and locally of finite presentation, a locally principal closed subscheme whose fibres are effective Cartier divisors is a relative effective Cartier divisor, and so is a finitely presented closed subscheme flat over S with such fibres (19.9). For X -> S smooth of relative dimension 1 and D a closed subscheme (Picard 3.1): if D is finite locally free over S it is a relative effective Cartier divisor; D is relative effective Cartier iff D -> S is locally quasi-finite, flat and locally of finite presentation, which implies locally quasi-finite and flat. The first implication is an equivalence when X -> S is proper, and the last one when S is locally Noetherian. Degrees add under sums (3.2), and D_1 inside D_2 gives D of degree d_2 - d_1 with D_2 = D_1 + D (3.3). Milne: D corresponds to (L(D), s_D) with L/sO_X flat over T (3.6). There is a fibrewise criterion (3.8). For C -> T proper smooth of relative dimension 1, D is relative effective iff finite and flat over T, and the image of a section is a relative divisor of degree 1 (3.9). Inclusion can be checked fibrewise (3.10).

nodes.statement: Hilb^d_{X/S}(T) is the set of closed subschemes Z of X_T that are finite locally free of degree d over T. It is an fpqc sheaf (2.1), limit preserving for X/S of finite presentation (2.2), and closed immersions induce closed immersions (2.3). It is separated if X/S is (2.4), and representable for affine X/S (2.5) and whenever any d points of a fibre lie in an affine open (2.6), for instance for quasi-projective f (2.7). For X -> S smooth of relative dimension 1 with all Hilb^d representable: Hilb^d x X -> Hilb^{d+1}, (D, x) |-> D + x, is finite locally free of degree d + 1 (3.4), and Hilb^d is smooth of relative dimension d (3.5). For X a geometrically irreducible smooth proper curve over a field k (3.6): Hilb^d_{X/k} is a smooth proper variety of dimension d whose K-points are the effective Cartier divisors of degree d on X_K; addition Hilb^{d_1} x Hilb^{d_2} -> Hilb^{d_1+d_2} is finite locally free of degree binom(d_1+d_2, d_1); and X^d -> Hilb^d is finite locally free of degree d!. nodes.title: Milne III 1.6, 1.13-1.14, 4.1-4.3: an abelian variety J with P^0_C -> J an isomorphism whenever C(T) is nonempty, glued from closed subvarieties of opens of C^(r) (r > 2g) and descended from a finite Galois extension
nodes.statement: Let C be a complete nonsingular curve over k. (1.6) There is an abelian variety J and a morphism iota: P^0_C -> J such that iota(T) is an isomorphism whenever C(T) is nonempty; (J, iota) is unique, and if P is in C(k) then J represents P^0_C (1.8). Construction (section 4, g > 0): fix r > 2g and use P^r_C = P^0_C via L |-> L (x) p^*L(rP). (4.1) A section of f: Div^r_C -> P^r_C would represent P^r_C by a closed subscheme of C^(r). (4.2) For an (r - g)-tuple gamma of k-points with D_gamma = sum P_i, C^gamma = {D : h^0(D_t - D_gamma) = 1} is open in C^(r). On P^gamma(T) = {L : h^0(L_t (x) L_gamma^{-1}) = 1} a section is built from the invertible sheaf q_*(L (x) p^*L_gamma^{-1}), which commutes with base change (I 4.2e) since h^1 = 0 by Riemann-Roch. If k is separably closed, the C^gamma cover C^(r). (4.3) P^gamma is represented by a closed subvariety J^gamma of C^gamma. After extending k so that the gamma_i are k-rational, glue the J^{gamma_i} along the open J^{gamma_i, gamma_j}. The result J represents P^r_C, is a group variety, and is complete because C^(r) -> J is surjective. (1.14) If 1.6 holds for C_{k'} with k'/k finite separable, it holds for C: the universal family gives a Galois descent datum on J', which descends by 1.13(a), and rigidified pairs fixed by the Galois group descend by 1.13(b).

nodes.title: Kleiman 4.8, 5.3-5.4, 5.19-5.20: Pic_{X/S} exists for X/S projective and flat with integral geometric fibres and represents the etale sheaf; Pic^0 is an open and closed subgroup of finite type, quasi-projective, and projective for geometrically normal X
nodes.statement: (4.8) If f: X -> S is projective Zariski locally over S and flat with integral geometric fibres, then Pic_{X/S} exists, is separated and locally of finite type over S, and represents Pic_{(X/S)(et)}. If moreover S is Noetherian and X/S projective, it is a disjoint union of open subschemes, each an increasing union of open quasi-projective S-schemes. (5.3) Over a field, if Pic_{X/k} exists and represents the fppf sheaf, then Pic_{X/k} is separated; it is smooth if it has a geometrically reduced open subscheme; and Pic^0_{X/k} is an open and closed subgroup scheme of finite type, geometrically irreducible, whose formation commutes with field extension. (5.4) If X/k is projective and geometrically integral, Pic^0_{X/k} exists and is quasi-projective, and it is projective if X is geometrically normal. (5.19) If Pic_{X/S} represents the etale sheaf and H^2(O_{X_s}) = 0, then Pic_{X/S} is smooth over a neighbourhood of s. (5.20) If the Pic^0 of the fibres are smooth of constant dimension, Pic^0_{X/S} is an open group subscheme of finite type; it is closed and proper if the fibres are complete and Pic_{X/S} is separated.

nodes.title: Milne I 1.1-1.5, 3.1-3.9: the rigidity theorem; pointed maps of abelian varieties are homomorphisms; commutativity; rational maps from nonsingular varieties into abelian varieties are regular; birational abelian varieties are isomorphic
nodes.statement: A group variety over k is nonsingular; a connected one is geometrically connected and irreducible. An abelian variety is a complete connected group variety. (1.1) If alpha: V x W -> U with V complete and V x W geometrically irreducible collapses V x {w_0} and {v_0} x W to u_0, then alpha is constant. (1.2) Every regular map of abelian varieties is a homomorphism followed by a translation. (1.4) The group law is commutative. (1.5) A morphism h: V x W -> A with h(v_0, w_0) = 0 decomposes uniquely as f p + g q. (3.1) A rational map from a normal variety to a complete one is defined outside codimension >= 2. (3.2) A rational map from a nonsingular variety into an abelian variety is regular, because (3.3) the indeterminacy locus of a rational map into a group variety is empty or of pure codimension 1. (3.4) Rigidity holds without completeness for maps from a geometrically irreducible product of nonsingular varieties into an abelian variety. (3.7) A rational map from a group variety into an abelian variety is a homomorphism followed by a translation. (3.8) Birationally equivalent abelian varieties are isomorphic. (3.9) Rational maps from A^1 or P^1 into an abelian variety are constant.
hypotheses: Milne's varieties are geometrically reduced separated schemes of finite type with nonclosed points omitted; the roadmap's definition (smooth, proper, geometrically connected group scheme over k) agrees with Milne's complete connected group variety (derived: a geometrically reduced group scheme of finite type over a field is smooth, and Milne shows connected group varieties are geometrically connected)
The general case of 3.1 uses the valuative criterion of properness (Hartshorne II 4.7); 3.3 uses divisors on the nonsingular V x V (AG chapter 12); 3.4 uses 3.5-3.6 (curves through a point are dense)
proofSteps: 1.1: over kbar, Z = q(alpha^{-1}(U - U_0)) is closed; for w outside Z, alpha(V x {w}) is a complete connected subvariety of the affine U_0, hence a point; by irreducibility alpha is constant.
1.2: apply 1.1 to (a, a') |-> alpha(a + a') - alpha(a) - alpha(a').
1.4: the inverse map fixes 0, so it is a homomorphism by 1.2.
3.2: combine 3.1 with 3.3.

nodes.title: Milne I 7.1-7.4: isogenies are finite, flat and surjective; n_A is an isogeny of degree n^{2g}, etale iff the characteristic does not divide n; A[n](k^sep) = (Z/n)^{2g} and T_l A is free of rank 2g; the structure of Ker(p) is stated
nodes.statement: (7.1) For a homomorphism alpha: A -> B the following are equivalent: alpha is an isogeny; dim A = dim B and alpha is surjective; dim A = dim B and Ker(alpha) is finite; alpha is finite, flat and surjective. Kernels are taken as group schemes (fibres in the sense of algebraic spaces). (7.2) If dim A = g and n > 0, then n_A is an isogeny of degree n^{2g}. It is etale in characteristic 0, and in characteristic p > 0 it is etale iff p does not divide n. (7.3) For k separably closed and p not dividing n, A_n(k) is free over Z/nZ of rank 2g; for l != char k, T_l A is free of rank 2g over Z_l ("One shows"), with an action of Gal(k^sep/k). (7.4) Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p, Ker(p) = (Z/pZ)^r x alpha_p^{2g-2r} x mu_p^r with 0 <= r <= g (stated).

Compare self-intersection numbers: (n_A^*D)^g = deg(n_A)(D^g) and n_A^*D = n^2 D, so deg n_A = n^{2g}.
Etaleness: (dn_A)_0 is multiplication by n on T_0 A, and homogeneity spreads the conclusion over A.

nodes.title: Milne I 8.4-8.14, 11.1: Pic^0(A), the dual abelian variety (A^vee, P) by its universal property, phi_L: A -> A^vee, the construction A^vee = A/K(L) (sketched in characteristic 0), polarizations and principal polarizations
nodes.statement: For L on A, K(L) = {a : (m^*L (x) p^*L^{-1})|_{A x {a}} trivial} is closed. Pic^0(A) consists of the L with K(L) = A, equivalently t_a^*L = L over kbar for all a, equivalently m^*L = p^*L (x) q^*L (8.4). The dual (A^vee, P) is defined by the universal property: P|_{A x {b}} is in Pic^0, P|_{{0} x A^vee} is trivial, and every family L on A x T with the same two properties is (1 x alpha)^*P for a unique alpha: T -> A^vee. It is unique, commutes with extension of scalars, satisfies A^vee(k) = Pic^0(A), and T_0 A^vee = H^1(A, O_A) (8.7). t_a^*L (x) L^{-1} lies in Pic^0 by the theorem of the square (8.8). Criteria for a divisorial correspondence to be a duality are 8.9 (proof cited to Mumford). For ample L, phi_L maps A onto Pic^0(A) (8.14, cited). In characteristic 0 over algebraically closed k, A^vee is constructed as A/K(L) with the universal property for normal parameter varieties; in characteristic p the notes refer to Mumford chapter III. A polarization is an isogeny lambda: A -> A^vee which over kbar has the form phi_L for an ample L; it is principal if deg lambda = 1 (section 11). For L invertible, deg phi_L = chi(L)^2, and chi(L) = (D^g)/g! for L = L(D) (11.1, cited to Mumford).

Summary 6.11: phi_{L(Theta)} is the canonical principal polarization, M_P = (f x 1)^*L'(Theta)^{-1}, L^P = (f x f)^*L'(Theta)^{-1}, and f^vee = -phi_{L(Theta)}^{-1}.
